alt: A table comparing three sources. Police recorded crime counts crimes reported and recorded under counting rules; it shows national trends but misses the dark figure. Victim surveys ask a random sample about crimes they suffered; they reveal unreported crime but miss corporate crime and homicide. Self-report studies ask people what offences they committed; they reveal hidden offending but miss serious and white collar crime.
caption: Each source sees a different part of crime, and each has its own blind spots.

alt: Four boxes, changes in counting rules, recording practice, police priorities and the law, all point to a change in recorded crime figures even when behaviour has not changed. Below, the 2014 withdrawal of National Statistics status and the later-2010s rise linked partly to better recording.
caption: Always ask whether a change reflects behaviour or recording.

alt: A flow from offence committed, through filter 1 (is it reported?) and filter 2 (is it recorded?), to the official statistics. Crime is lost at filter 1 if the victim does not know, care, feels afraid or distrusts the police, and at filter 2 through police discretion, lack of evidence or recording rules. Victim surveys and self-report studies each reach some of the lost crime.
caption: The dark figure is crime lost at reporting or at recording, not unsolved crime.

alt: A timeline. 1982: the British Crime Survey begins. Mid-1990s: CSEW estimates of crime peak, then fall over two decades for crimes such as burglary. 2012: renamed the Crime Survey for England and Wales. Mid-2010s: fraud and computer misuse added. Later 2010s: police recorded crime rises, partly because of better recording.
caption: Survey crime fell from the mid-1990s; recorded crime’s later rise partly reflects better recording.

alt: Five numbered steps for describing crime data: state the overall direction, quote the start and end figures, note any exception or turning point, calculate a difference or percentage change if asked, then ask whether the change reflects behaviour or recording.
caption: Describe the numbers first, then question what they really measure.
